newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Angry Romanians denounce government plant closures.
newsitem.headline: Angry Romanians denounce government plant closures.

text.p: Thousands of Romanians denouncing the government and the IMF poured into streets and blocked rail lines on Friday to protest against plans to close loss-making factories in the latest phase of market reform.

The mainly peaceful protests erupted throughout the country a day after Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea announced a list of 17 plants suffering chronic losses to be closed down rapidly at the urging of the International Monetary Fund.

Up to 5,000 shouting protesters outside the town hall in the oil-producing town of Ploiesti, 60 km (35 miles) north of Bucharest, where refineries are slated for closure. They demanded Ciorbea provide them with an explanation.

"Traitors, traitors!" "You sold us to the IMF!" protesters shouted, punching the air with their fists outside the grim concrete building erected during the 25-year rule of Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu. "Come and talk to us!"

One poster held aloft portrayed Ciorbea and President Emil Constantinescu as puppets on strings being pulled by the IMF. Workers said they found refinery gates closed on Friday, and were given no explanations. "Oilmen, unite!" they shouted.

"What the Americans couldn't do with wartime bombs, this government is doing now," said one man, referring to Allied bombing raids on the Ploiesti oilfields when Romania was allied with Nazi Germany. "They are destroying our oil industry."
Two junior ministers rushed to Ploiesti to discuss the closure of the Petrotel and Vega refineries with local officials.

The oil industry, with huge excess capacity from the communist era, has been singled out as one of the country's most inefficient sectors. Other plants on the hit list are in the chemical and food processing industries.
In other protests, the state Rompres news agency said 3,000 industrial workers had pushed trucks and other equipment in front of the city hall in the Danube River port of Braila.
In Cluj, in the heart of the central Transylvania region, 1,200 workers said they would remain in their metal plant until they received more information about its inclusion on the list.
Leaders of the Prahova county council in Ploiesti were particularly incensed at the timing of the announcement, only days after flooding caused widespread damage in the area.

Fifteen km (nine miles) east of Ploiesti, in the wine-producing town of Valea Calugareasca, dozens of employees of a chemical plant also due to be closed sat on rail lines and blocked a Moscow-bound express train from early morning.
About 300 passengers, mainly Russians and Ukrainians returning from Bulgarian seaside holidays, were trapped with little to eat or drink. Many passed the time playing chess.
"We have no food, no water, no information," said Andrei Boinov, a Moscow pianist. "Why can't officials do something?"
Police took no action. The Interior Ministry warned it would intervene "as the situation requires".
Ciorbea, speaking on Thursday at the end of a month-long IMF assessment of reforms, said water, power and other services would be cut to the plants due to be closed.
But a spokesman for the state power utility said no such order had been received, at least for the oil refineries.
The government launched reforms after defeating leftists in last year's elections. It won IMF praise for curbing inflation, which fell to a record monthly low of 0.7 percent in July.

The leu currency is largely stable, foreign reserves are on the rise and the government revised the budget to keep the deficit within IMF limits. But Ciorbea admitted that closure of loss-making industry had been delayed for too long.
